extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, jurors, and patent litigators using model jury instructions in U.S. patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for determining infringement and invalidity in U.S. patent litigation, including statutory standards (pre-AIA and AIA), burdens of proof, and doctrines such as anticipation, prior use, on-sale bar, and inherency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability under 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant intended for components to be combined into a product that would have infringed a claim of the patent if combined in the United States; actual combination need not have occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to find that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, as long as the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed a claim if combined in the United States. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2); WesternGeco; Microsoft v. AT&T; Cardiac Pacemakers; Waymark; Rotec.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by import, sale, offer for sale, or use of product made by patented process (35 U.S.C. § 271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(g), the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) the defendant imported/sold/offered for sale/used a product made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim, (2) the product was made between the patent issue date and expiration/date of trial, and (3) the defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between those dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether the evidence establishes the product was 'made by' the claimed process. If the product was materially changed by later processes, or is only a trivial or non-essential part of another product, then it was not 'made by' the claimed process. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 271(g); Amgen v. Roche; NTP v. Research In Motion; Mycogen v. Monsanto; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This burden never changes regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (pre-AIA) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes certain items received into evidence: products/methods publicly known or used by others in the U.S. before the claimed invention was invented; products/methods in public use or on sale in the U.S. before the cutoff date; patents issued before the cutoff date; publications publicly accessible before the cutoff date; and products/methods made in the U.S. before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the parties' identified prior art admitted into evidence. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA).) Practice Note: identify factual issues (date, public availability) for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (AIA) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes anything patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of the claim; and patents/applications naming another inventor filed before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes AIA-specific statutory references (35 U.S.C. § 102 as amended by AIA; §100(i)). Practice Note: identify to the jury disputes over date/public availability and related issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to prior art (AIA and pre-AIA) — disclosures by inventor or derived disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if it was made by the inventor or obtained from the inventor; other exceptions apply if the subject matter was disclosed earlier by the inventor or was owned/subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statutory exceptions under §102(b) and (c) (pre-AIA) and §102(b)(1) (AIA) should be applied and explained to the jury when factual issues exist as to derivation, common ownership, or inventor-originated disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of whether PTO considered a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner, the challenger must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PTO did not have all material facts, the challenger's burden may be easier to sustain. Jury may be instructed to evaluate whether evidence is materially new as opposed to previously considered by the PTO. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity analysis for independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims do not refer to other claims and must be read separately; dependent claims refer to and include all elements of the claim(s) they depend from. Each asserted claim must be evaluated separately for invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid; however, if a dependent claim is invalid, the independent claim from which it depends must also be found invalid. (Cites: Comaper v. Antec; Callaway v. Acushnet; Ormco v. Align Tech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the time of the invention/effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art must be evaluated from the perspective of such a person as of the relevant date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 103; KSR; Continental Can v. Monsanto.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — single-reference requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation, the defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that the claimed invention is not new because each element in the claim is present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation. Consider what a person of ordinary skill would have understood from the particular reference. Practice Note: instruct the jury on inherency if alleged. (Cites: Net MoneyIN v. Verisign; Toro v. Deere; other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference can inherently anticipate if the missing element or feature would necessarily result from what the single item teaches to persons of ordinary skill; but inherency requires that the feature necessarily is present, proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence outside the prior art reference (including experimental testing) may be used to show inherency, but likelihood is not sufficient—necessity is required. Prior unrecognized uses may still anticipate if the feature was necessarily present. Give inherency instructions when alleged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA) — standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly known by others in the United States before the date of invention (pre-AIA cutoff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the date of invention or priority is disputed, instruct the jury on how to determine the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a) (pre-AIA); case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (AIA) — standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the claimed invention was available to the public before the effective filing date of the claim (AIA standard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual disputes implicate the §102(b) and (c) exceptions (e.g., disclosures within one year by inventor or derived from inventor), instruct the jury on those exceptions. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) — elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention was publicly used by others in the U.S. before the invention date or more than one year before U.S. filing date (pre-AIA), rendering the claim invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention was publicly used in the U.S. if an embodiment was (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the U.S., and (2) ready for patenting. Factors: nature of activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation, testing circumstances. Secret third-party use is not public unless public/employees had access. Ready for patenting = reduced to practice or sufficiently detailed drawings/descriptions enabling one of ordinary skill. (Cites: numerous Fed. Cir. cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (AIA) — worldwide standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date, rendering the claim invalid under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same factors as pre-AIA for public use and readiness for patenting apply; instruct jury on relevant §102 exceptions if factual issues arise. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar (pre-AIA and AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if, before the applicable cutoff/effective filing date, an embodiment of the claimed invention was the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA limited to U.S. sales), and the invention was ready for patenting at that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by accepting the offer. The invention is 'subject of a sale or offer' if embodied in an actual product commercially sold or offered for sale, even if confidential; no actual sale required. Readiness for patenting requires reduced to practice or sufficiently specific drawings/descriptions. Practice Note: address §102(b) exceptions when factual disputes about inventor-origin disclosures exist. (Cites: Pfaff v. Wells Elecs.; Helsinn; Medicines Co.; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A public use or sale does not count against patentability if it was experimental — a legitimate effort to test claimed features or determine if the invention works — provided the primary purpose was experimentation and it was by or under the control of the inventor or assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentation must relate to claimed features and aim at technological improvement rather than commercial exploitation; incidental profit is permissible. Experimentation by third parties for their own purposes does not qualify. If defendant proves prior public use/sale, burden shifts to plaintiff to show experimental purpose; if plaintiff's evidence is strong enough, the prior use/sale may not constitute invalidating public use or sale. (Cites: City of Elizabeth v. Nicholson; Polara Eng'g; Clock Spring; Allen Eng'g; LaBounty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a printed publication (maintained in tangible form) before the effective filing date/invention date/more than one year before U.S. application (as applicable) and was sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tangible forms include printed pages, electronic files, microfilm, photographs, Internet publications, photocopies. Accessibility means persons interested and ordinarily skilled, exercising reasonable diligence, could locate it. The disclosure must be enabling so one of ordinary skill could use the invention without undue experimentation. If accessibility is disputed, give additional instruction defining 'publicly accessible.' (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§102 pre-AIA and AIA; Blue Calypso; Orion IP; In re Lister; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) — anticipation by another's invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was invented by another person in the U.S. before the patentee (and not abandoned, suppressed, or concealed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence either (1) the third party reduced to practice a product/method including all features of the claim before the patentee, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence to reduce to practice. Prior invention may be negated if abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If abandonment/suppression/concealment is at issue, define those terms for the jury. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(g) pre-AIA; Teva v. AstraZeneca; Rosco v. Mirror Lite; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (pre-AIA) — anticipatory effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was previously patented in the U.S. or a foreign country before the relevant cutoff (pre-AIA), e.g., before the patentee's invention date or more than one year before U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the date of invention or priority is disputed, instruct the jury on how to determine the date of invention or deliver the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §102 pre-AIA; Advanced Display; In re Carlson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (AIA) — anticipatory effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the U.S. or a foreign country before the effective filing date of the claimed invention under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues exist concerning whether disclosure in a patent resulted from disclosure by the inventor/joint inventor or from another who obtained it from the inventor, instruct the jury on §102(b)(1) exceptions as needed. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. §§102(a)(1) & 102(b)(1).)
